Each wrong guess shrinks the possible range. Start with a midpoint like a country starting with M, N, or O. The hint eliminates roughly half the alphabet in one shot. Second guess cuts another chunk. Where players usually go wrong

Neither does mint牙膏 or those aggressively bright mint greens used in sports branding. The name points you in the right direction but demands calibration against actual visual output.

Another trap: assuming all greens cluster together in guessing priority. After Highlighter yellow yesterday, some players may be overcorrecting toward saturated brights. This color punishes that instinct—it's muted and deliberate, not shouting for attention.

Is Mint Green the same as sage or seafoam?

Close, but not identical. Sage typically runs slightly lighter and more gray-green. Seafoam leans more toward teal territory with higher blue values. Something in the medium-dark, slightly muted green range works well as a first probe. Avoid extremes—neither near-white pastels nor near-black shadows. A mid-intensity green with some gray influence gives you the cleanest initial reading. From there, adjust saturation and lightness based on the score feedback before chasing minor hue shifts.

colorfle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Today's Colorfle puzzle tests your understanding of how red, green, and blue light combine to produce a target color. If you've been guessing without a system, the reveal probably felt frustrating. Here's how a careful reader approaches the mix.

Colorfle answer today: how the mix should be read

The core mechanic asks you to identify three source colors that, when mixed additively, recreate the target shown on the board. Think television pixels, not art class paint. Red plus green yields yellow. Green plus blue produces cyan. All three together hits white. Reading the target means breaking down its RGB percentages into three components that sum to those values. Players who start with the dominant channel usually narrow their options faster than those who treat every color as equally likely.

What the source colors are telling you

Each clue widget on today's page represents a potential source color. A careful player checks whether the hints eliminate certain channels or suggest proportions. If a hint shows low blue values, that color probably isn't contributing heavily to the final mix. Archive links from previous days show patterns—some targets favor warm tones (high red and green), others skew cool (elevated blue). You don't need to memorize every combination, but noticing which channels appear most often in successful solves sharpens your eye for the next board. The solver tool can confirm your reasoning if you're stuck on a specific ratio.

Why additive color logic beats random mixing

Random guessing treats each color as equally viable. Additive logic treats the puzzle as a math problem with visual feedback. When you see a target leaning toward magenta, you know red and blue dominate the mix. When the result looks neutral gray, all three sources sit closer to equal intensity. Players who internalize this relationship solve faster and waste fewer guesses on colors that can't mathematically contribute to the target. The reveal card confirms whether your breakdown matched reality. If it didn't, trace back which channel you misread—that's where the learning happens.

Easy adjustment path for the next Colorfle

Before your next attempt, review what went wrong today. Did you overestimate a channel? Underestimate another? Adjust your starting hypothesis accordingly. Some players find it helpful to write down the target's approximate RGB split before looking at the source options. Others cross-reference the archive to see if similar targets appeared recently. Either way, the solver link on this page lets you test combinations without burning additional guesses. Use it as a sanity check rather than a crutch—the pattern recognition builds faster when you work through it manually first.

Questions players keep asking

Does the order of my three color selections matter?

No. Additive mixing is commutative—red, green, blue in any sequence produces the same result. What matters is getting the right three colors with the correct intensity levels.

Can I reuse a color more than once in the same solution?

Standard Colorfle rules require three distinct source colors. Reusing the same color twice would effectively reduce your equation to two variables, which rarely matches the target's complexity.

What happens if my mix overshoots a channel value?

The reveal flags overshoot errors clearly. If your combined red value exceeds the target's red component, the puzzle registers that as incorrect. Each source contributes its full value—you can't partially apply a color.

Are there patterns in daily targets that repeat over time?

The archive shows some recurring tendencies—certain hue families appear more frequently than others—but the game cycles through enough variation that pattern-matching alone won't guarantee solves. Understanding the underlying color math remains essential.

Contexto measures proximity through meaning, not spelling. Every guess receives a numerical rank based on how semantically close it sits to the hidden answer. Lower numbers mean you're circling the target; higher numbers signal you've wandered into related but distant territory.

Contexto answer today: what the rank pattern usually means

The rank you see after each guess isn't arbitrary. It reflects a calculated distance in the semantic space the game maintains. A guess landing in the top 50 typically sits within one conceptual hop of the answer. Numbers climbing past 500 suggest you've shifted into a connected but broader category.

Watch how ranks compress as you narrow in. Early guesses might jump from 847 to 234 to 89—a compression pattern indicating you're closing distance. If ranks plateau despite fresh attempts, you've likely exhausted that semantic vein and need a different angle entirely.

A useful habit: note which guess dropped your rank most dramatically. That word revealed a pathway closer to the answer's core concept. The archive on this page tracks historical patterns if you want to study how similar compressions played out on previous days.

When to pivot categories instead of forcing synonyms

Players often exhaust themselves chasing synonyms when the smarter move involves category shifts. If you've submitted five variations of the same root word and ranks keep hovering in the same range, synonym hunting has hit diminishing returns.

Consider moving upstream. Instead of "happy," try "emotion." Instead of "car," try "transportation." These broader categorical jumps sometimes leapfrog over the dead zone where more specific synonyms live. The game rewards understanding the answer's domain, not perfecting its vocabulary.

Pivoting doesn't mean guessing randomly. It means recognizing that your current semantic cluster has been mapped and finding a new entry point. Sometimes the path runs through an unexpected door—related industries, component materials, or the answer's opposite before circling back.

Why broad words beat clever words here

Cleverness rarely pays off in Contexto. The game rewards breadth over wit. A simple, general term will almost always outperform an obscure alternative that technically shares meaning.

Think about it this way: the algorithm maps concepts, not vocabulary sophistication. "Dog" gets you further than "corgi." "Music" outperforms "symphony." General terms cast wider nets in semantic space, increasing your odds of landing near the answer's coordinates.

This surprises players who approach Contexto like a crossword. Crosswords reward niche knowledge; Contexto punishes it. Save the specialized vocabulary for later guesses once you've bracketed the answer's territory. Lead with the obvious, the common, the unremarkable word that captures the broadest version of your thought.

How to cut tomorrow's guess count

Today's board teaches lessons for tomorrow's play. After the reveal, review which of your early guesses landed lowest. Those words identified the correct semantic neighborhood. Now ask yourself: could you have reached the answer faster by pursuing that cluster differently?

Most players waste guesses on specificity too early. Tomorrow, lead with three broad categorical terms before drilling down. This establishes your position relative to the answer rather than guessing blindly and triangulating backward.

The solver linked on this page can help you reconstruct the distance map if you want to study the full ranking sequence. Some players find it useful to compare their guess order against the official solution path archived in the history.

Questions players keep asking

Does the game use dictionary definitions or contextual usage?

Contexto leans heavily on how words function in practice, not just their dictionary entries. A word's associations—what it commonly appears near in text, media, and conversation—matter more than formal definitions. This is why "beach" might rank closer to "vacation" than "sand," depending on usage patterns.

The hint widget reveals partial information about the answer without giving it away entirely. Use it when you're genuinely stuck, not as a shortcut. Players who lean on hints too heavily miss developing the semantic mapping intuition that makes later puzzles easier. Treat hints as diagnostic tools, not crutches.

Why did the guess rank worse even though it seems more relevant?

Semantic relevance doesn't always align with intuitive relevance. The game's model weighs factors you can't see—co-occurrence patterns, cultural associations, and trained embeddings. What feels obviously related might sit at a surprising distance in the model's space. Trust the rank more than your gut feeling.

Is there a maximum number of guesses allowed?

Contexto doesn't impose a hard limit, but the daily format encourages efficiency. Players who finish in fewer guesses typically developed better starting strategies. The archive tracks completion metrics if you're curious how your guess count compares to historical averages.

Once you identify the answer, the game confirms your success and displays your final rank. You can then explore the full distance chart showing every guess you made and its corresponding position. The reveal doesn't erase your data—you can still study the session afterward.

Once you've pinned continent and hemisphere, population and area become precision tools. Population tells you where a country sits in the development spectrum within that region. A country with 80 million people isn't automatically a major power; it's mid-tier globally but might dominate its region. Context matters more than the raw number.

Dotadle answer today: which hero clues carry the most weight

Primary attribute clues usually land hardest. When the puzzle flags Strength, Agility, Intelligence, or Universal heroes, that's your first hard filter—125+ heroes just became irrelevant. Attribute placement narrows the field more aggressively than almost any other single clue. If you're ignoring it, you're wasting the most powerful tool on the board.

Lore snippets and ability names tend to be mid-tier signals. They confirm candidates you've already narrowed down rather than finding them from scratch. An ability name like "Shadowraze" points hard at Shadow Fiend once you've got the attribute locked. Without that attribute context, it could fit a dozen heroes with similar wordplay.

The fastest solvers work subtraction first. Open the solver tool and input whatever attribute data appears on today's card. That alone cuts the roster by two-thirds. From there, layer in lane assignment if it's listed—some heroes genuinely can't jungle or trilane effectively, and Dotadle knows it.

Attack type (Melee vs Ranged) is another fast filter hiding in plain sight. Most players scan past it. Combined with primary attribute, you can often isolate a pool of six to twelve candidates in under thirty seconds.

Ability count matters too. Heroes with four abilities behave differently than those with three plus an ultimate toggle. If the puzzle specifies ability quantity, use it. It's a clean boolean filter that doesn't require you to know what those abilities do.

When roles help and when they mislead

Dota 2 heroes have flexible lane assignments in actual games, but Dotadle treats role labels as valid puzzle data. Treat them accordingly—but don't over-index. A hero labeled "Support" might also dominate midlane in certain drafts. The puzzle knows this. That's why role clues often appear alongside other qualifiers.

If a role clue stands alone, treat it as a suggestion rather than a definition. Cross-reference it against attribute before locking in. A Strength Support narrows differently than an Intelligence Support, even if both share the same lane tag.

Some players get baited by patch-specific offlane or roaming picks. Today's Dotadle likely uses current roster data, but older archives may reflect different meta eras. Check the archive if you're pulling historical context and notice mismatches between role labels and hero pools.

Smarter way to approach tomorrow's Dotadle

Build a personal shortlist before you hit the board. Memorize which heroes fall into each attribute bucket—not perfectly, just well enough to spot the outliers. Universal heroes are the newest category and trip up even experienced players. Spend five minutes reviewing that list tonight.

On solve day, resist the urge to guess from memory. Let the clue stack guide you instead. Attribute first, then range, then role. Only reach for hero names when the pool drops below fifteen. The solver exists for a reason—use it as a safety net, not a crutch.

Reviewing yesterday's puzzle helps more than you'd expect. Patterns repeat. If you missed a clue type today, flag it for tomorrow. The solver history on this site tracks your recent sessions, so you can spot recurring weak points without maintaining a spreadsheet.

Yes. Universal heroes appeared in Dota 2 after the attribute rework and Dotadle reflects that. Treat Universal as a separate filter alongside Strength, Agility, and Intelligence. If the puzzle lists it, use it—don't fold Universal heroes back into the other categories.

Today's puzzle follows that pattern well. The initial still rewards players who notice background details rather than lead actors. That famous shot—the one you've seen on posters and in compilations—can pull your guess toward a different film entirely if it's visually similar to today's answer. How to clean up tomorrow's Framed in fewer reveals

The fastest route to a one-reveal solve isn't talent—it's process. Before you even load tomorrow's puzzle, decide what you're looking for. Not the title. The category. Period, genre, and production country narrow dramatically from a single glance at the first still.

Build your mental checklist: era markers first, then costume silhouettes, then background signage or technology. If you see flip phones, you're pre-2012. If you see specific car models, you've got a year within five years. These anchors are faster than any keyword search once you train your eye.

The archive link on today's page lets you review past puzzles and track which frame positions tend to appear when. Why does the first frame sometimes show a scene I've never seen?

Players who rely on IMDb searches early develop slower pattern recognition than those who work from visual clues alone. Save external research for puzzles you've exhausted through pure observation.

The difficulty curve doesn't shift by time of day. What changes is your own state—morning players tend to be sharper on visual detail; evening players often perform better on narrative-heavy stills. Play when your focus is highest, not when the algorithm supposedly serves easier puzzles.

Why do some puzzles repeat visual styles across days?

Which swaps usually unlock two words at once

Efficient solving comes down to finding the letter that fixes a horizontal and vertical word simultaneously. In a standard six-word grid, the center intersection often holds the key. Moving a single tile into that central slot can turn two yellow markers green in one action. This is the highest-value move available on any board.

Look for vowels sitting in consonant-heavy slots or vice versa. If an 'E' is trapped in a spot that demands a 'T', and that 'T' is currently blocking the 'E's true home, swapping them immediately resolves both lines. Novice players tend to fix one word completely before touching the crossing line. This approach wastes the opportunity to use crossing letters as free hints.

Target the intersections first. Once the center holds firm, the outer edges usually fall into place with minimal friction. The solved grid above demonstrates this; notice how the middle row and middle column share a critical character that stabilizes the entire structure.

Panic swapping is the primary move killer. When the timer ticks or the move counter dips, the urge to drag random yellow tiles grows strong. This rarely works. Every drag consumes a turn, and blind shuffling often breaks a partially formed word that was actually correct.

Another common leak involves ignoring the green anchors. Some solvers treat green tiles as decorative rather than structural. They pull a correct letter out of position to test a hunch, only to spend two more moves putting it back. Trust the green. If a letter is locked, build around it, not through it.

Over-committing to a single word also drains resources. You might get five letters of a six-letter word perfect, but if the sixth letter breaks a crossing word, you haven't gained ground. The board state remains unstable. Step back and look at the grid as a single interconnected system rather than six separate anagrams.

Resist the urge to fill in common short words like 'THE' or 'AND' until the crossing letters force your hand. These flexible words can fit almost anywhere, making them poor anchors for the early game. Let the difficult, constrained words dictate the board layout first.

Today's Wordle Answer Revealed

The solution for Wordle #2629 on June 4, 2026, is ALLOY. This five-letter word fits the pattern of starting with a vowel and closing with a consonant sound represented by Y. It contains a repeated letter pair that often trips up players who expect unique characters in every slot.

Why This Word Fits Today's Puzzle

Tracy Bennett's selection of ALLOY follows a recent trend of tangible, physical nouns. After yesterday's NOTCH and the day before's BASIS, the puzzle leans into words you can hold or measure. The double L creates a specific structural hurdle. Many solvers burn their second guess on words like ALERT or ADORE, missing the repeated consonant entirely. The Y ending also narrows the field significantly, eliminating common plural forms that end in S. This combination forces a shift from common verb patterns to specific noun structures.

Meaning and Everyday Use

An alloy is a substance formed from the combination of two or more metals. Steel serves as the most common example, mixing iron with carbon to increase strength. Brass combines copper and zinc, while bronze mixes copper with tin. You encounter alloys daily without thinking about them. The ring on your finger likely contains gold mixed with harder metals to prevent scratching. Airplane frames rely on aluminum alloys to stay light yet durable. The term implies improvement through mixture, suggesting the whole is stronger than its individual parts.

How to Work Toward the Answer

Start by testing common vowels early. If you hit the A in the first spot, resist the urge to fill the rest with random consonants. Look for words that test double letters quickly. Pools, bells, or falls can reveal that repeated L structure. If your first guess reveals the A and Y but misses the middle, avoid words with S or T. Those letters appeared frequently in the previous three days (BASIS, NOTCH, CHILI). The puzzle often rotates away from high-frequency consonants immediately after a heavy run. Focus on softer consonants like L, M, or R for your follow-up guesses.

Best Starter Ideas for This Puzzle

Words like ADIEU or ARISE remain solid openers because they front-load vowels. For a puzzle like this, where the answer starts with A, a starter like CRANE or SLATE works well to eliminate common consonants. If you prefer to target the double letter mechanic early, try a word like BELLY or FOLLY. These sacrifice vowel coverage to test the repeated consonant hypothesis immediately. See our full list of best starting words for Wordle to optimize your first move. The goal is to confirm or deny the double letter presence by guess two.

Recent Wordle Pattern Notes

The last week has shown a distinct preference for concrete nouns over abstract concepts. ETUDE, CHILI, BASIS, and NOTCH all describe specific things or defined measures. ALLOY continues this streak. We have also seen a cluster of words with repeated letters, with CHILI featuring a double I and now ALLOY with a double L. This suggests the editor is comfortable with non-unique letter sets. Check the Wordle archive to see how often double letters appear in past months. Recognizing these clusters helps adjust your strategy for future puzzles.

Extra Tips for Keeping a Streak Alive

Don't panic when you see a repeated letter. Many players waste a guess trying to force unique letters into every slot. If you suspect a double, commit to it. Use a word that places the suspected pair in different positions if you aren't sure where they sit. Also, remember that Y functions as a vowel here, but it sits at the end. This limits the number of valid candidates significantly. Review our advanced strategy guide for more on handling tricky letter distributions. Consistency comes from adapting to the specific constraints of the day, not relying on a rigid system.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the definition of ALLOY?

An alloy is a metal made by combining two or more metallic elements, especially to give greater strength or resistance to corrosion. Common examples include steel, brass, and bronze.

Does ALLOY have any repeated letters?

Yes, the letter L appears twice in the word. It occupies the second and third positions.

How many vowels are in the answer?

There are two vowels: A and O. The letter Y acts as a consonant in this specific word structure, though it often functions as a vowel in other contexts.

What are some good second guesses if I start with A?

If your first guess confirms the A, try words like ULTRA, OCTAL, or LOCAL to test other vowel placements and common consonants. Avoid reusing the L immediately unless you are specifically testing for the double letter.

worgle-answer-today.articleHtml:
If you're staring at today's Worgle board wondering where to go next, the Welsh alphabet plays by different rules than English. Today's answer contains letters that frequent Welsh vocabulary far more than standard five-letter English words—particularly combinations involving W, Y, and DD that trip up players expecting typical Wordle behavior.

Worgle answer today: what the Welsh letter pattern is hinting at

Welsh uses some letters sparingly in English contexts but dominates here. A careful player notices that W and Y appear in roughly one out of every three valid Worgle answers—sometimes as vowels, sometimes consonants, often both depending on position. The double-D combination (written as DD) shows up regularly too, sounding like an English "th" and appearing in words that would never pass in standard Wordle.

Today's puzzle likely follows this pattern. Check the reveal card above for the confirmed answer, then cross-reference against your remaining guesses. If you've got a W or Y in the right spot, that's your anchor—build around it rather than second-guessing based on how English typically distributes these letters.

How to read common Welsh digraphs without overforcing them

The biggest mistake players make with Worgle is treating Welsh spellings as phonetic puzzles when they're actually orthographic ones. Welsh digraphs like CH, DD, FF, NG, LL, PH, RH, and TH each represent single sounds, but they function as distinct letters in the game. That means a word containing "DD" occupies two tiles just like any other two-letter sequence—no special treatment.

A few patterns worth knowing: CH sounds like a strong Scottish "loch" and appears in roughly 4% of solutions. LL sounds nothing like English—it resembles a hissed "l" and shows up in surprisingly common words. RH starts silent, so "rhododendron" begins with an R-sound despite the H sitting there. None of this changes your guessing strategy, but recognizing these combinations helps you parse green/yellow feedback faster.

Use the solver tool on this page if you're stuck on a specific position. It accounts for Welsh letter distribution in ways generic Wordle solvers don't.

Where English guessing habits break the solve

Every Wordle veteran brings assumptions that work against them in Worgle. The most damaging: treating Q, X, and Z as rare letters. In Welsh, Q and X rarely appear—but Y functions as a full vowel much more often than in English, and W frequently appears in positions where English would never place it.

Another trap: assuming vowel patterns match English distribution. Welsh has fewer pure vowel letters (A, E, I, O, U) available per word because W and Y absorb so many vowel roles. If your guess uses three of the five standard vowels, you might be working from an English mental model that's actively misguiding you.

Players also struggle with DD vs. TH. Both represent similar sounds to English ears, but DD appears in Welsh words where English would never use TH. Don't eliminate DD just because TH didn't work in a previous puzzle—this alphabet operates independently.

How to handle tomorrow's Worgle more smoothly

Build your opening guesses around Welsh letter frequency, not English norms. Words heavy in W, Y, and DD serve better as diagnostic tools early. A starting word like WYNND or BYDDD won't exist, but constructing five-letter sequences that test these letters gives you cleaner information than relying on ESTON or CRANE.

Bookmark the Worgle archive linked on this page. After each puzzle, note which letters appeared and where. Over a week, you'll see patterns emerge that make future solves faster. Players who treat each day's puzzle in isolation miss the cumulative advantage of studying Welsh letter behavior.

When you're genuinely stuck, run your best candidates through the solver before burning guesses. It factors in Welsh-specific constraints that catch errors before you commit to an impossible line.

Questions players keep asking

Is W treated as a vowel in Worgle?

Mechanically, no—it's just another letter tile. Phonetically, yes—W often represents a vowel sound in Welsh (like in "cwm"). This dual nature is why W appears so frequently in solutions. Don't hesitate to use it as a vowel substitute when your English instincts tell you to hunt for A, E, or I instead.

Why does my solver suggest words that aren't accepted?

Generic Wordle solvers use English dictionaries. Worgle uses a Welsh word list that includes valid Welsh terms English dictionaries reject. If your external solver isn't configured for Welsh vocabulary, it will propose words the game won't accept. Stick to the solver built into this page—it's calibrated for today's word list.

No. Like standard Wordle, only common Welsh words appear as solutions. Place names, names of people, and borrowed English words generally don't qualify. Stick to native Welsh vocabulary for your guesses.

Does the hard mode in Worgle work the same as regular Wordle?

Yes—the hard mode constraint carries over identically. Any revealed correct letter must stay in that position for all subsequent guesses. The difference is purely linguistic: you're locked into Welsh letter positions rather than English ones, which trips up players unfamiliar with Welsh spelling patterns.

worldle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Today's Worldle puzzle presents a familiar trap: the shape looks like several countries at once. A careful player who starts with continent elimination instead of border-tracing almost always reaches the answer faster. The silhouette alone narrows things down to two or three possibilities before any directional hint appears.

Worldle answer today: what the silhouette should suggest first

Before touching the compass rose or reading the distance percentage, study the overall shape. Is it tall and thin or wide and squat? Does it have a distinctive peninsula jutting out? Is there a visible island attached? These features filter by continent immediately. A long north-south orientation with no coastal indentation screams Africa or South America more often than players realize. The solver on this page lets you input confirmed continents to surface matching candidates, which cuts the blind guessing phase entirely.

The reveal card shows today's answer above, but players arriving mid-puzzle can still learn from the pattern. Every Worldle silhouette rewards geographic intuition over memorization. The players who solve consistently aren't the ones who've memorized every border—they're the ones who know which continent shapes cluster together.

How direction and distance clues narrow the shape

Once you've pinned the continent, the directional arrow becomes your primary tool. If the mystery country sits northeast of your last guess, that eliminates everything south and west of your current position. Combined with the distance percentage—how close you are geographically—the puzzle collapses quickly for anyone paying attention to relative positioning rather than absolute coordinates.

The percentage hint deserves more weight than most players give it. A 90% match means you're practically standing on the right country; a 40% match means you're looking at the wrong continent entirely. Players who chase border similarities while ignoring distance percentages waste guesses on visual resemblances that don't matter geographically.

For tomorrow's puzzle, practice reading the compass before the silhouette. Ask yourself: if this were Europe, what runs northeast of my mental map? That habit builds faster than memorizing flags or capitals.

Why neighboring countries become the easy wrong answer

The most common mistake on Worldle is locking onto a neighbor before using the directional clue. Two countries can share a border, look vaguely similar from a distance, and sit in completely different directions from your starting guess. The puzzle deliberately exploits this pattern—players see France-shaped and reach for Belgium, Netherlands, or Switzerland before checking whether those countries even fall in the hinted direction.

Neighboring countries also share coastlines, mountain ranges, and cultural associations that make silhouettes deceptively similar. The Pyrenees define both Spain and France, but the directional arrow separates them instantly. Always confirm direction before committing to a neighbor guess.

The archive link on this page tracks recent puzzles. Reviewing yesterday's solution reveals how often the correct answer sat adjacent to a tempting wrong choice. That pattern recognition compounds over time.

How to finish tomorrow's Worldle with fewer detours

Tomorrow's puzzle benefits from tonight's preparation. Spend five minutes reviewing one region's geography—Southeast Asia, the Balkans, West Africa—rather than cramming global facts. Deep familiarity with a smaller area pays dividends when that region rotates into the daily puzzle.

Build a mental checklist before each guess: continent confirmed, direction checked, distance percentage reviewed. Skip any guess that doesn't satisfy all three criteria. This sounds mechanical, but it prevents the emotional attachment to visually pleasing shapes that leads players down dead ends.

Players who maintain a simple error log—even just noting which guess category failed them—improve faster than those relying on pattern matching alone. The answer archive provides historical context for tracking your own accuracy trends.

Questions players keep asking

Does the distance percentage work differently for small countries?

Yes. The percentage measures geographic center-to-center distance, so tiny nations show bigger jumps between guesses. Moving from Vatican City to Italy registers as a larger shift than moving from Russia to Kazakhstan, despite the latter covering vastly more territory.

Can I reset my daily streak if I fail a puzzle?

Worldle tracks consecutive solves separately from the main streak counter. Missing a day breaks the calendar streak but doesn't affect your solve accuracy history. Check the stats page to see both metrics independently.

Why does the directional arrow sometimes point away from obvious geography?

The compass measures direction from your guessed country to the mystery country, not the reverse. If you're guessing east of the answer, the arrow points west toward it. Many players flip this relationship and interpret the hint backwards.

Are continent filters available in the mobile version?

The mobile interface includes the same continent selector as the desktop version. Tap the globe icon near the guess input to filter by region before submitting. This feature works offline once the puzzle loads.

How does Worldle select tomorrow's country?

The puzzle cycles through regions algorithmically, ensuring broad geographic distribution over time. No country repeats until the full rotation completes. This means obscure nations appear roughly as often as major ones.
